What does a derivative tell you?

The derivative \(f'(x)\) is a new function giving the gradient at each input where the tangent has a finite slope. For a power, \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}\) where the derivative exists.

How do roots and reciprocals differentiate?

For positive x, use \(\sqrt{x}=x^{1/2}\) and \(\frac{1}{x^p}=x^{-p}\). Keep the original domain when differentiating.

How does the sign describe the curve?

If \(f'(x)>0\) on an interval, f increases there. If \(f'(x)<0\), f decreases. A zero derivative at one point gives a horizontal tangent.

The curve is \(y=x^2\). Find its height and gradient at \(x=1\).

Substitute into the curve to obtain \(y=1^2=1\). The point has coordinates \((1,1)\).

Differentiate the power \(x^2\) to obtain \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2x\).

Set \(x=1\) in the derivative to get gradient \(2\). The curve passes through \((1,1)\) with tangent slope \(2\).

addmaths-0606-d1-chain-rule.description: Identify the inner function before differentiating a composite power, root or reciprocal.

sections.title: Which function is inside the other?
sections.label: Inner outer

blocks.html: Set \(u=g(x)\) and \(y=F(u)\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm du}\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}\).

figure.alt: Input x becomes the inner value u, and the inner value becomes the output y.
figure.caption: For \(u=2x+1\) and \(y=3u^2\), a change in \(x\) travels through both links. Multiply the derivative factors.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
1. Choose the inner expression \(u\) before differentiating.
  2. Apply the power rule to y as a function of u.
  3. Multiply by \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}\) and substitute the original inner expression.

blocks.title: Find the complete chain-rule derivative
blocks.prompt: Give the derivative of \(y=2(3x-1)^3\).
blocks.hint: Differentiate the cube while keeping the bracket, then multiply by the derivative of the bracket.
blocks.solution:
The outer derivative is \(6(3x-1)^2\). The inner derivative is \(3\).

The result is \(18(3x-1)^2\).

retry.feedback: The bracket changes by 3 units each time x increases by one. Include the factor of 3.

blocks.html: The outer power rule alone gives the rate per unit of the bracket, not the rate per unit of x.

blocks.title: Differentiate an outer power with an inner function
blocks.prompt:
The function is \(f(x)=11 \left(3 x + 4\right)^{2}\).

Find the gradient at the specified input. Use \(x=3\).
blocks.hint: Complete the gradient function before substituting the stated input.
blocks.solution:
Substitute \(3\) into \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\) after differentiating.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\big|_{x=3}=858\)

Answer: \(858\).

retry.feedback: The derivative of the inner function must multiply the outer derivative.

sections.intro: Imagine building the expression in two steps. The inner function produces the input for the outer function. Each step contributes a rate.

sections.title: What if the outer operation is a root?
sections.label: Square root

blocks.html: If \(u>0\), the derivative of \(\sqrt{u(x)}\) is \(\frac{u'(x)}{2\sqrt{u(x)}}\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
1. Write the square root as a power of one half.
  2. Differentiate the bracket separately and keep its sign.
  3. Substitute only after the complete derivative has been formed. Use a positive inner value wherever the formula has a square root in its denominator.

blocks.title: Check the sign of a root gradient
blocks.prompt: Find the gradient of \(y=5\sqrt{6-2x}\) at \(x=1\).
blocks.hint: The bracket slope is negative. Use it in the numerator.
blocks.solution: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{5(-2)}{2\sqrt{6-2x}}\). At \(x=1\), this is \(-\frac{5}{2}\).

retry.feedback: The inner derivative is −2, so the curve is falling where the derivative is defined.

blocks.html: A root can be defined at an endpoint where the derivative formula has a zero denominator.

blocks.title: Differentiate an outer power with an inner function
blocks.prompt:

Find the gradient at the specified input. Use \(x=0\).
blocks.hint: Evaluate the numerator and square-root denominator of the derivative separately.
blocks.solution:
Substitute \(0\) into \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\) after differentiating.

\(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\big|_{x=0}=0\)

Answer: \(0\).

retry.feedback: The derivative of the inner function must multiply the outer derivative.

sections.intro: Writing a square root as a power makes both parts of the chain rule visible. Check the inner value before you evaluate the result.

sections.title: How does an outer reciprocal change the sign?
sections.label: Reciprocal

blocks.html: For \(u(x)\ne 0\), \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\bigl(u(x)^{-1}\bigr)=-\frac{u'(x)}{u(x)^2}\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html:
1. Express the reciprocal as a power of −1.
  2. Apply the chain rule and carry both signs.
  3. Keep the excluded values from the original denominator.

blocks.title: Keep the outer minus sign
blocks.prompt: For \(y=\frac{4}{x+1}\), find the gradient at \(x=3\).
blocks.hint: The power −1 gives a negative multiplier when differentiated.
blocks.solution: \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac{4}{(x+1)^2}\). At \(x=3\), the gradient is \(-\frac{4}{16}=-\frac14\).

retry.feedback: The denominator is squared, but the minus sign from the outer power remains.

blocks.html: Squaring the denominator cannot make an excluded input valid.

blocks.title: Differentiate an outer power with an inner function
blocks.prompt:
The function is \(f(x)=\frac{2}{\left(7 x + 8\right)^{2}}\). Work where \(7 x + 8>0\).

Find the gradient at the specified input. Use \(x=3\).
blocks.hint: Find the value of the denominator after differentiating. Keep the inner multiplier and the sign from the negative power.
blocks.solution:
Write \(y=2(7x+8)^{-2}\). Multiply the outer derivative \(-4(7x+8)^{-3}\) by the inner derivative \(7\).

Thus \(y^\prime=-\frac{28}{(7x+8)^3}\). At \(x=3\), \(y^\prime=-\frac{28}{29^3}=-\frac{28}{24389}\).

solution: Put \(u=7x+1\), \(y=4u^2\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=7\) and \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm du}=8u\).

examples.title: Find the gradient at a particular input
examples.question:
The function is \(f(x)=11 \left(7 x + 1\right)^{3}\).

Find the gradient at the specified input. Use \(x=4\).
solution: Put \(u=7x+1\) and \(y=11u^3\). Then \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm du}=33u^2\) and \(\frac{\mathrm du}{\mathrm dx}=7\).
The gradient function is \(33u^2\cdot7=231(7x+1)^2\). At \(x=4\) the gradient is \(231(29)^2=194271\).

examples.title: Explain why the gradient is zero at the origin
examples.question:
The function is \(f(x)=11 \sqrt{x^{2} + 5}\).

Find the gradient at the specified input. Use \(x=0\).
solution: Use \(u=x^2+5\) and \(y=11\sqrt u\). Multiplying \(\frac{11}{2\sqrt u}\) by \(2x\) gives \(y^\prime=\frac{11x}{\sqrt{x^2+5}}\).
At \(x=0\), the numerator is zero and the denominator is positive. The gradient is therefore zero.

revision.body:
Which factor stays unchanged?

For a product \(y=uv\), use \(y'=u'v+uv'\). In each term differentiate one factor and keep the other.

How do you differentiate a root factor?

For \(y=u\sqrt v\) with \(v>0\), \(y'=u'\sqrt v+\frac{uv'}{2\sqrt v}\).

What if both factors need the chain rule?

If \(u=A^m\) and \(v=B^n\), the two product terms are \(mA^{m-1}A'B^n\) and \(A^m nB^{n-1}B'\).

Quick worked example

A curve has equation \(y=\left(x + 10\right)^{2} \left(12 x + 8\right)\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

Write \(u=(x+10)^2,\ v=12x+8,\ u^\prime=2(x+10),\ v^\prime=12\).

Use \(u^\prime v+uv^\prime=2(x+10)(12x+8)+12(x+10)^2\).
revision.checks:
• Multiplying the two derivatives omits the size of both original factors.
  • In the second product term, keep the whole original polynomial.

revision.body:
Which product comes first?

For \(y=\frac{u}{v}\), with \(v\ne0\), \(y'=\frac{vu'-uv'}{v^2}\).

Where is a quotient defined?

The original quotient requires \(v(x)\ne0\). Any equivalent expression and its derivative inherit that restriction.

How can a bracketed numerator stay readable?

Use the chain rule to obtain \(u'\) before substituting it into \(\frac{vu'-uv'}{v^2}\).

Quick worked example

A curve has equation \(y=\frac{x^{2} + 1}{x + 3}\).

Find \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\).

  1. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-7 + \frac{- x^{2} + 2 x \left(x + 3\right) - 1}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\)
  2. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=9 + \frac{- x^{2} + 2 x \left(x + 3\right) - 1}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\)
  3. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{- x^{2} + 2 x \left(x + 3\right) - 1}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\)
  4. \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=- \frac{- x^{2} + 2 x \left(x + 3\right) - 1}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}\)

Here \(u=x^2+1,\ v=x+3,\ u^\prime=2x,\ v^\prime=1\). The original domain excludes \(x=-3\).

Use \(\frac{(x+3)(2x)-(x^2+1)}{(x+3)^2}\). Simplifying gives \(\frac{x^2+6x-1}{(x+3)^2}\), option C.
revision.checks:
• Reversing the numerator terms changes the sign of the gradient.
  • Even where a factor cancels, the point with original denominator zero is missing.
revision.examTip: Use a complete bracket before squaring a multi-term denominator.

revision.body:
How does change in x give change in y?

For a small signed input change \(\delta x\) near \(x=a\), use \(\delta y\approx f'(a)\delta x\).

When do you add the change?

Use \(f(a+\delta x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)\delta x\) for the new output.

How can you check a reciprocal estimate?

For \(f(x)=\frac1x\), the tangent estimate near \(a\ne0\) is \(f(a+h)\approx \frac1a-\frac{h}{a^2}\).

Quick worked example

The quantity \(y\) is given by \(y=7 x^{2} + 6 x + 4\). The input changes from \(6\) to \(\frac{607}{100}\).

Estimate \(\delta y\) using a derivative.

At \(x=6\), \(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=90\). Multiply by \(\delta x=\frac{7}{100}\).

Answer: \(\frac{63}{10}\).

revision.body:
How does a constraint remove a variable?

For a rectangle against a wall with fixed length L of fencing, \(A=x(L-2x)\) for \(0<x<\frac L2\).

Which root describes a feasible tray?

For a square sheet of side s, \(V=x(s-2x)^2\), with \(0<x<\frac s2\).

What makes a stationary value the greatest in the model?

Use \(f'(a)=0\) to identify an interior candidate. Prove its nature using derivative signs or \(f''(a)\), then check the whole feasible range.

Quick worked example

An enclosure against a wall uses \(24\,\mathrm m\) of fencing along its three exposed sides. Find its greatest area.

If the two perpendicular sides each have length x, the parallel side has length \(24-2x\). Thus \(0<x<12\).

\(A=x(24-2x)=24x-2x^2\). Then \(A'=24-4x=0\) at \(x=6\).

Since \(A''=-4\) and the area tends to zero at both boundaries, \(x=6\) gives the greatest area.

The area is \(6(12)=72\,\mathrm{m^2}\).
